title: One Bible, Two Americas: How Slavery Tested the Way Americans Read Scripture
standfirst: Culture and the Bible in Antebellum America
subtitle: The democratic, common-sense reading of the young republic, Stringfellow's plain-text case for slavery, the abolitionists' appeal to the spirit of Scripture, the Exodus as the enslaved read it, Douglass's two Christianities, the Slave Bible of 1807, and Mark Noll's verdict on a hermeneutic that could not settle the question.

sections.title: A Nation of Bible Readers
sections.body:
In the decades after independence, the United States became one of the most Bible-saturated societies the modern world had seen, and it read the book in a way all its own. The Second Great Awakening filled the frontier with Methodist circuit riders and Baptist farmer-preachers who needed no seminary to open the text, and the American Bible Society, founded in 1816, set out to put a copy in every household. The historian Nathan Hatch has called the result the democratization of American Christianity. Authority moved away from learned clergy and inherited creeds toward the ordinary reader, who held a Bible in one hand and a republican conviction in the other: no bishop or professor had the right to tell a free man what the text meant.

Underneath that confidence lay a philosophy most Americans never knew they held. The Common Sense Realism of the Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid, taught across American colleges, held that the unprejudiced mind perceives reality directly and reliably. Applied to Scripture, it yielded a hermeneutic of the plain sense. The Bible means what an honest reader sees on its surface, and a reading that needs history or subtlety to work is probably an evasion. Mark Noll has traced how this alliance of Protestant biblicism, common-sense philosophy and democratic individualism became the working theology of the young republic.

There was real good in it. It honored the Reformation's conviction that Scripture belongs to the people, and it gave farmers and enslaved preachers alike a right to read that no hierarchy could revoke. But it carried an assumption that would prove ruinous. It took for granted that what seemed plain to an American reader was simply what the text said, as though the reader brought nothing to the page. In 1861 a nation of Bible readers went to war over what the Bible plainly taught.

sections.title: The Plain Text for Slavery
sections.body:
In 1841 Thornton Stringfellow, a Baptist minister in Virginia, published a pamphlet examining the testimony of Scripture on slavery, and it was reprinted and enlarged in the years that followed. Its method was the method of the age, and that is what made it formidable. Stringfellow walked through the canon in order. The patriarchs held servants, and God blessed Abraham without rebuking him. The law of Moses, in Leviticus 25, permitted Israel to buy bondmen from the surrounding nations and to leave them to their children as an inheritance. Jesus lived among Roman slavery and did not denounce it. The apostles, in Ephesians 6 and elsewhere, told slaves to obey their masters, and Paul sent the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon. Each text, read at its surface, seemed to say that slaveholding as such was no sin.

It is a mistake, and a comfortable one, to imagine that this argument persuaded only the cynical. It persuaded because it used the very rules evangelical Americans had been taught to trust. If the plain sense governs, and the plain sense of Leviticus 25 permits perpetual bondage, then the abolitionist who calls all slaveholding sin appears to be correcting God. Southern divines pressed exactly that point. A man who adds to Scripture a moral law it does not contain, they argued, has made his own conscience into a second Bible. Even in the North, Charles Hodge of Princeton wrote in 1836 that the New Testament did not treat slaveholding as sinful in itself, however much he wanted its cruelties reformed.

What the argument could not see was itself. It rarely asked whether Hebrew debt servitude or Roman household slavery was the same institution as the hereditary racial chattel of the cotton South. Nor did it notice that its plain reading kept arriving where the reader's economy already stood. Interest seldom announces itself. It makes some texts feel obvious and others feel strained.

sections.title: The Spirit Against the Letter
sections.body:
The abolitionists answered from another part of the same book. Some fought on the proslavery ground and won exchanges there. Theodore Dwight Weld's The Bible Against Slavery, published in 1837, set the protected, time-limited servitude of the Mosaic law beside the plantation and found almost nothing in common, and abolitionists pointed again and again to the law in Exodus 21 that made stealing a man a capital crime. But the heart of the antislavery case lay elsewhere, in what its advocates called the spirit of the gospel. Jesus commanded that we do to others what we would have them do to us. Paul told the Athenians, in Acts 17:26, that God made from one man every nation of mankind. The whole movement of Scripture, from the Exodus through the prophets to a church in which there is neither slave nor free, bent away from bondage. Read by that trajectory, the regulations of Leviticus were concessions to hardness of heart, as Jesus said of the divorce law in Matthew 19, and no charter for Virginia.

This was the better reading. It read the parts by the whole and the law by its fulfillment, as the church's wisest interpreters had done since Augustine. In the American setting, though, it carried a heavy cost. To a common-sense reader, an appeal to the spirit over the letter sounded like a confession that the letter was against you. Some abolitionists confirmed the suspicion. As the conflict hardened, a radical wing grew willing to say that a Bible which sanctioned slavery could not be the word of God, and the defenders of slavery gladly cast themselves as the guardians of scriptural authority against infidelity.

So the stronger exegesis lost the argument it should have won. It needed a slower, more historically trained reading than the culture had learned to trust, and the culture had been taught that slowness was a symptom of evasion.

sections.title: The Exodus From Below
sections.body:
Another community was reading the same Bible, and its readings were rarely printed in the pamphlet wars. Enslaved Christians in the South were commonly barred by law from learning to read, and after Nat Turner's revolt in 1831 several states tightened those laws further. They received Scripture largely through the ear, from white preachers paid to teach obedience and from their own preachers in the gatherings the historian Albert Raboteau called the invisible institution, worship held at night in cabins and brush arbors beyond the master's hearing.

What they heard there, they heard as their own story. Israel was a people in bondage, Pharaoh a master who would not let them go, Moses a deliverer sent by a God who heard the groaning of slaves. The spirituals sang Go Down, Moses and asked whether the Lord who delivered Daniel would not deliver every man. This was typology of the kind the church had practiced since the fathers, the Exodus read as a pattern of salvation, but it refused the spiritualizing that would have left the chains untouched. Deliverance meant the soul, and it meant the body too.

These readers were also selective, and they knew why. Howard Thurman, the great twentieth-century Black theologian, recalled that his grandmother, born into slavery, would not have him read Paul's letters to her, apart from the chapter on love, because the master's preacher had used Paul's words on slaves and masters against her for years. She had heard a canon edited by power and answered with a canon edited by pain.

Both sides selected. Only one side owned the other. The enslaved read from beneath the text's weight, and from there the Exodus looked like what it was: the founding act of a God who frees slaves.

sections.title: Two Christianities
sections.body:
When Frederick Douglass published his Narrative in 1845, seven years after his escape from slavery in Maryland, he knew what some readers would conclude. A book that showed slaveholders praying, class-leading and whipping in the same week would be taken as an attack on religion itself. So he added an appendix. In it he explained that his words were aimed at the slaveholding religion of his country and not at Christianity properly so called. He drew a line between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ, said that he loved the second because it was pure, peaceable and impartial, and said that he could only hate the first because it was corrupt, partial and hypocritical. In the South, he observed, the bell of the slave auction and the bell of the church rang out together.

Then he did something the theologians of both sections rarely managed. He let Scripture judge the culture rather than the culture judge Scripture. He set before his readers the twenty-third chapter of Matthew, Jesus's woes against the scribes and Pharisees who tithe mint and neglect justice, and let it stand as a portrait of the slaveholding religion he had known.

The hermeneutical importance of that appendix is easy to miss. Douglass was not a trained exegete, and he did not pretend to be. What he possessed was a vantage point. He had been the property the slaveholding reading defended, and from there he could see that the plainness of the proslavery text was a property of the reader's location, not of the page. His distinction kept the Bible and the slave on the same side by recovering Christ from the people who claimed him, which is exactly the work this whole sorry chapter required, and the work almost nobody with a pulpit was doing.

sections.title: The Bible With the Exits Removed
sections.body:
The proslavery reading had a cruder cousin on the other side of the Atlantic, and it shows the logic with unusual candor. In 1807, the same year Parliament abolished the British slave trade, a book was printed in London under the title Parts of the Holy Bible, Selected for the Use of the Negro Slaves, in the British West-India Islands. It was produced for the Society for the Conversion of Negro Slaves, an Anglican body working in the Caribbean colonies, and it is now usually called the Slave Bible.

Its editors did with scissors what the American pamphleteers would do with emphasis. Large portions of Scripture were simply left out. The account of Israel's deliverance from Egypt was removed. Galatians 3:28, with its declaration that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, was missing. The texts that told slaves to obey their masters stayed in. A planter could hand this book to the people he owned and feel that he had given them the word of God.

The excisions are an accidental confession. Whoever chose them read the Exodus more accurately than Stringfellow and his successors claimed to. They knew which stories would teach an enslaved reader that God takes the side of slaves, and they knew which verse would make the master and the slave equals at the Lord's Table, so they cut them. The Slave Bible is a British artifact, made for the Caribbean rather than Virginia, and it should not be made to carry American guilt. But it isolates the mechanism. Every culture that reads Scripture to protect its arrangements is tempted to edit the canon. Most do it without scissors, by deciding which passages are preached, which are memorized and which are quietly treated as obscure.

sections.title: What the Hermeneutic Could Not Settle
sections.body:
In The Civil War as a Theological Crisis, published in 2006, Mark Noll argued that the war exposed more than a moral failure. It exposed a failure of method. Both North and South largely shared the same Reformed, literal, common-sense way of reading, and that method, applied in good faith by sincere people, could not produce agreement on the most pressing moral question in the nation's life. The plain sense of Leviticus pointed one way, the spirit of the gospel another, and the American hermeneutic had no agreed way to adjudicate between them. Noll's bitter observation is that the question of what the Bible taught about slavery was finally decided not by theologians but by the Union's generals.

Noll also showed what the American debate kept failing to examine. Many Protestant and Catholic observers abroad could grant that Scripture tolerated some forms of servitude and still see that American slavery, hereditary and defined by race, was something the Bible never described. That argument was the most promising one available, and it gained remarkably little ground at home. The reason was race. On both sides of the Mason-Dixon line, assumptions about Black inferiority were so widely held that the distinction between biblical servitude and racial chattel slavery seldom felt urgent. The culture had decided the question before the exegesis began.

Abraham Lincoln saw the deadlock from the presidency. In his Second Inaugural Address, in March 1865, he said of the two sections, "Both read the same Bible and pray to the same God, and each invokes His aid against the other." He did not pretend the two causes were morally equal. He did refuse to pretend that the Almighty belonged to either.

sections.title: Inside the Indictment
sections.body:
I am an American Baptist pastor, and I cannot read this history from a safe distance. Stringfellow was a Baptist. The Baptists of the South separated from their Northern brethren in 1845 over whether slaveholders could be appointed as missionaries, a year after the Methodists divided over a slaveholding bishop. The plain-sense, every-man-his-own-interpreter reading of Scripture that made the proslavery case feel unanswerable is my own inheritance. I was taught to trust it, and I still do, more than is safe.

The lesson is not that the Bible is unclear. It is that we are. A text does not become plain in a vacuum; it becomes plain to a particular reader standing somewhere, and where he stands decides which verses feel obvious and which feel like special pleading. The Bible was not silent in those years. Douglass heard it. The enslaved heard it in the Exodus. The spirit-and-trajectory readers heard it, even when they argued badly. What failed was a culture that mistook its own interests for the plain sense and could not imagine that it was reading from anywhere at all.

That is a harder judgment than condemning the dead. It means asking which texts feel plain to me now because they cost me nothing, and which feel strained because they would cost me a great deal. It means reading with the people who stand beneath the text's weight, with the whole canon rather than the favorite shelf, and with the long church rather than the present congregation. And it means admitting that I would very likely have read Leviticus 25 the way my neighbors read it.

They had the same Bible we have. What we owe them is the suspicion that we are not so different.
